candidate_row.report_series: NASA Office of Inspector General interim memorandum
candidate_row.report_edition: Published June 24, 2026; interim, not a completed audit
candidate_row.period_label: September 2024 contract change and April 2026 stop-work observation, reported June 24 2026
candidate_row.summary: NASA OIG reported the historical conversion to cost-plus-award-fee and an April 2026 stop-work order. The reported $1.9 billion is contract value, not recognized revenue, remaining backlog or cash. The interim memorandum does not establish current October status or formal contract termination.
candidate_row.excerpt:
Then in
September 2024, citing difficulties administering a development project with a firm-fixed-price contract
type, NASA converted HALO to a cost-plus-award-fee contract, increasing the combined value of the
contract to $1.8 billion and delaying delivery of the module to October 2026. However, in April 2026, the
Agency issued a stop work order to Northrop Grumman for its work on the HALO contract. By then, the
value of the contract had risen to $1.9 billion and Northrop Grumman was working to address corrosion
throughout HALO’s primary structure, which would significantly impact the project’s schedule.

candidate_row.report_series: NASA Office of Inspector General interim memorandum
candidate_row.report_edition: Published June 24, 2026; interim, not a completed audit
candidate_row.period_label: Counterfactual completion projections in the June 24 2026 interim memorandum
candidate_row.summary: Only if HALO continued to completion, OIG projected July 2031 delivery and Gateway operation no earlier than 2032. These are counterfactual projections, not current delivery or launch dates. The agency response contests the architectural assumptions; the audit was not complete.
candidate_row.excerpt:
If Northrop Grumman was to continue HALO to completion, in our judgment, the overall contract costs
would have continued to rise and the delivery schedule would have been further delayed. Based on
trends in Northrop Grumman’s monthly schedule reporting data over the past 1.5 years since the
contract was converted to cost-plus, we project the HALO would not have been delivered to NASA until
July 2031, a 6-year delay. Moreover, given the additional time to integrate the HALO module with the
Power and Propulsion Element pre-launch, as well as the approximately 10 months needed to reach its
designated lunar orbit, we estimate that Gateway would not have been operational until at least 2032.
Due to the projected end date far into the future and limited availability of contractor monthly financial
management reports, we were unable to perform a complete cost projection for HALO.

candidate_row.report_series: NASA Office of Inspector General interim memorandum
candidate_row.report_edition: Published June 24, 2026; interim, not a completed audit
candidate_row.period_label: NASA management response to the interim memorandum, as published June 24 2026
candidate_row.summary: NASA management said the projections for the systems covered by the memorandum relied on past performance under outdated architectural assumptions. This is the agency response, not independent validation of the revised architecture or evidence that the earlier stop-work observation was conditional.
candidate_row.excerpt:
While the OIG’s
                    projections indicate that continuing these systems would likely increase total lifecycle cost,
                    NASA stresses that these projections rely on past performance under outdated architectural
                    assumptions that do not reflect the Ignition Day principles of discipline, affordability,
                    simplification, and speed.
